query: What the Yearbook Keeps The yearbook committee has your page in proof, with the lines they mean to print under your portrait. You may let them stand or strike them out. "Two at most," says the editor, a second-year with ink on her nose. "We're short of room." Let them print your fame You leave the line about the Ledger's special edition. The editor looks relieved; it was her favourite. Let them print the line about you Someone has written "The one you went to when it mattered." You don't know who. You leave it. Let the shadow stand In the proof, the candles behind your portrait have gone out. The editor offers to retouch it. You tell her to leave it as it is. Keep the line about your thesis The line about your thesis on the founders' seal has been half struck through already, in the headmistress's hand. You un-strike it. Strike them all You strike out every line. The editor sighs and prints your name and the year, and nothing else. It suits you, somehow.
